title: The southern map
hook: India to Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Java

segments.voice: Yesterday, rediscovery: scholars far away reading texts that Buddhists had kept all along. Your line was read again. What did you go back to? Today, we step back and look at the whole map. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

Put your finger on the plain of the Ganges, where the Buddha walked and taught. Now slide it south, down the long coast of India, across a narrow strait to the island of Sri Lanka. From there, swing east across the Bay of Bengal to Myanmar. Keep going into Thailand, up the river to Laos, down into Cambodia, and out across the sea to the island of Java. For many weeks this path has been walking that line one place at a time. Today, the whole southern map at once.
screen: `THE GANGES PLAIN.` → `SOUTH TO THE ISLAND.` → `EAST ACROSS THE BAY.`

segments.voice: First stop, India, where it began, with councils of monks gathering to keep the teaching straight and an emperor, Ashoka, sending messengers outward. Second, Sri Lanka. The island's chronicles say Ashoka's son, the monk Mahinda, brought the teaching there, and a cutting of the Bodhi tree followed. The island became a keeper of the Pali texts. Third, the mainland: Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. Here the teaching traveled with monks, with traders, and with kings who built and gave. We met Sukhothai's walking Buddhas, the smiling towers of Angkor, and the saffron line at dawn in Luang Prabang. Fourth, the sea road to Java, where Borobudur rose as a mountain of carved stone. Now notice what the map does not show. A line on a map looks like one clean journey. It wasn't. The teaching moved back and forth, over a long time. Monks from the mainland sailed to Sri Lanka to be ordained again, and carried the lineage home. Kings sent for texts and teachers. Some places took up other forms of Buddhism, and some, like Java, later took up other faiths. Today the Theravada tradition, the way of the elders, lives on in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, and its monks chant the same Pali texts. A monk in Colombo and a monk in Vientiane can recite the same verses in the same old language. That shared voice is the southern road.
screen: `INDIA: COUNCILS AND AN EMPEROR.` · `SRI LANKA: MAHINDA AND THE TREE.` · `THE MAINLAND: MONKS, TRADERS, KINGS.` · `THE SEA ROAD TO JAVA.` · then, large: `THE SOUTHERN ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trace the southern road on a map. If you have a map or a phone nearby, find India, then Sri Lanka, then follow the coast east. If not, draw it in the air with one finger, slowly. Then let the hand rest and the breath settle. With each breath, name one stop to yourself: India. Sri Lanka. Myanmar. Thailand. Laos. Cambodia. Java. When you reach the end, start again, and let each name be one quiet breath. The bell holds the time.
Theravada. The way of the elders, living on in Sri Lanka and across Southeast Asia, chanting the same Pali texts. Today's word.
Your line: the southern road. Today, when you travel anywhere, even across town, notice what you carry with you that came from somewhere else. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Theravada monks in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia chant the Pali texts daily, and monks from these countries have long visited and ordained in one another's monasteries.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism went south once, in a straight line.
what it means: it traveled by monks, traders and kings, and kept moving back and forth.
what a scholar hears: lineages were renewed across the sea, so the southern lands share a Pali canon and keep reviving one another.

notes: Mahinda's mission and the Bodhi tree cutting (brought by Sanghamitta in the chronicles) are attributed to the island's chronicles; confirm framing.

'Monks from the mainland sailed to Sri Lanka to be ordained again': general claim about lineage renewal (e.g. Burmese and Thai ordinations in Sri Lanka, and later Sri Lankan ordinations from Thailand and Burma). No dates given under the claims rule; confirm.
'Theravada is the main form of Buddhism in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia': confirm this is acceptable without a statistic.
Java's later conversion mentioned briefly and neutrally; confirm tone.
